description: Our team seeks to develop robust solutions to address the impacts of the El Niño phenomenon on crops, using valid data and rigorous analysis to support decision-making and establish clear, measurable, and achievable goals. Our objective is to transform information into concrete actions that strengthen agricultural resilience, reduce risks, and generate a real and sustainable impact on affected communities.
summary:
Every farming season, farmers face the same question: what should I grow next? GAIA answers it. GAIA is a decision-making simulator for crop rotation that turns NASA satellite data into clear, climate-informed guidance for farmers, agronomists, the agricultural industry and government agencies.

It combines decades of NASA data (POWER, GLDAS, IMERG, SMAP) with SENAMHI rainfall and stations, soil characteristics (texture, organic carbon and pH), and FAO and INIA crop data, including crop coefficients (Kc) that reveal each crop’s water demand. GAIA corrects rainfall bias, computes evapotranspiration (FAO-56) and delivers 24-month forecasts with uncertainty ranges, ENSO scenarios, water balance and frost risk.

Rotation protects soil, saves water and cuts risk, yet one wrong choice can cost a whole season. GAIA puts the climate ahead on the farmer’s side. We piloted it in Junín, Peru, and South Park, Colorado, its climatic counterpart, and the approach can scale worldwide. Rigorously validated and fully reproducible, it offers a forecast you can believe.
details:
What it does and how it works. GAIA is a decision-making simulator for crop rotation, built for professional farmers, agronomists, the agricultural industry and government agencies. It runs on a monthly climate database spanning decades (since 1950) for two regions with identical structure: Junín, Peru (10 analysis points) and South Park, Colorado, USA (9 points). For each point it combines rainfall, reference evapotranspiration (ET0), temperature, soil moisture, soil characteristics (texture, organic carbon and pH), terrain, land cover and vegetation (NDVI). From this, GAIA delivers 24-month forecasts with 80% uncertainty intervals, climate scenarios (current, neutral, El Niño and La Niña), water balance (P/ET0), frost-risk classes and crop yield simulation with AquaCrop, the FAO crop model. Users explore everything through an interactive 3D globe with NASA satellite layers.

Data used. From NASA we used POWER, GLDAS, GPM IMERG, SMAP, MODIS, SRTM and Daymet, plus NASA GIBS imagery layers. We added ERA5-Land, SoilGrids, ESA WorldCover and Sentinel-2. From SENAMHI we used PISCOp rainfall and the HUAYAO, JAUJA and INGENIO stations. For crops we used FAO EcoCrop (crop ecological requirements), the USDA Cropland Data Layer for South Park, the Regional Directorate of Agriculture of Junín (provincial production 2022 and sowing campaigns 2009-10 to 2019-20), and INIA crop coefficients (Kc).

Benefits and intended impact. Crop rotation protects soil, saves water and reduces risk, but choosing what to plant requires anticipating the climate and the crop’s water and yield response. GAIA delivers that information clearly, helping reduce costly planting decisions and use water better. Built on open satellite data, it can scale worldwide; for now we focus on our region, Junín, and on Colorado, chosen for its climatic similarity to Junín.

Tools and technologies. We used Google Earth Engine and NASA POWER to obtain data, and Python (pandas, numpy, statsmodels, scipy) for processing, calibration and modeling. We applied FAO-56 Penman-Monteith for ET0, SARIMAX, SARIMA and Ridge regression for forecasts, and AquaCrop (AquaCrop-OSPy) for yield simulation. The web application uses Three.js and WebGL (globe.gl) with administrative boundaries from geoBoundaries, GADM and Natural Earth. The pipeline is automated and reproducible on a standard computer, running in 15 to 30 minutes.

What makes it creative. GAIA unites global satellite data, local Peruvian station data, soil information, crop requirements and a crop model in one tool, and presents them on an interactive globe. It also uses a US region climatically similar to Junín as a reference to compare and validate the method. Every forecast comes with its uncertainty range.

Factors our team considered. We corrected rainfall bias with local data: in Junín, bias dropped from +45.1% to −1.6%. We calibrated temperature with stations, kept calibration and validation data separate, and verified station and point locations. We also accounted for the high correlation between points in the same region, evaluating results by region. The team combines Environmental Engineering (data and models) and Systems Engineering (application).
